entry: Middle Indo-Aryan language, studied as the sacred language of [[Theravada|Theravada Buddhism]] and the language of the Tipiṭaka, the canon of early Buddhist texts. The name does not appear in the canonical literature and seems to have arisen in commentaries, perhaps from a misunderstanding of the phrase *pāli-bhāsa*. Early commentaries identified Pali with Magadhi, the language of the kingdom of [[Magadha]] in what is now [[Bihar]]. Modern scholars instead regard Pali as a mix of several Prakrits from around the 3rd century BCE, partly Sanskritized, with no attested dialect that has all its features. It descends from dialects that differed from Ṛgvedic Sanskrit and probably originated in western India, though it retains some eastern features. It ceased to be a spoken vernacular by the early centuries CE. The Government of India designated Pali a classical language on 3 October 2024.

Standard collection of Theravada Buddhist scriptures, preserved in [[Pali]]. Known as the Tipiṭaka, or three baskets, it is the most complete extant early Buddhist canon. It is divided into the Vinaya Piṭaka, on monastic discipline; the Sutta Piṭaka, the largest, containing discourses attributed to [[The Buddha|the Buddha]]; and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, treatises elaborating doctrine, particularly about the mind. The Vinaya and Sutta Piṭakas closely resemble the texts of other early schools, while the Abhidhamma is distinctively Theravada. Tradition holds that the teachings were recited at a council after the Buddha's death and preserved orally before being written down. The earliest surviving canonical Pali fragments date only to the mid-5th to mid-6th century CE, in the [[Pyu city-states]] of Burma. Buddhaghosa, active in the 4th–5th century, wrote commentaries that summarize the traditional interpretation, most fully in his *Visuddhimagga*.

Strait between southeastern India and northern Sri Lanka, linking the Bay of Bengal to the Laccadive Sea. It is about 137 km (85 mi) long and 64–137 km (40–85 mi) wide, and it is named after Robert Palk, governor of Madras from 1755 to 1763. Its southern boundary is a chain of low islands and shoals called Ram Setu or [[Adam's Bridge]]. In the Hindu epic [[Ramayana]], the shoals were said to be part of a bridge built by the army of [[Rama]] to rescue [[Sita]] from [[Ravana]]. The strait is shallow near the shoals, typically 1–3 m (3 ft 3 in–9 ft 10 in) deep, and reaches a maximum of 35 m (115 ft). Large ships find passage difficult, although fishing boats navigate it. A shipping channel was first proposed to the British government of India in 1860, and a 2005 canal project met opposition on religious grounds.

Rare, lustrous silvery-white metal and [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with atomic number 46 and symbol Pd. English chemist William Hyde Wollaston discovered it and named it after the asteroid 2 Pallas, itself named for an epithet of the Greek goddess [[Athena]]. Palladium, [[Platinum]], [[Rhodium]], ruthenium, iridium and osmium form the platinum group metals, which have similar chemistry. Palladium has the lowest melting point and is the least dense of them. It is soft and ductile, does not tarnish in air, and dissolves readily in [[Aqua regia|aqua regia]]. More than half of supply goes into [[Catalytic converter|catalytic converters]], which convert as much as 90% of harmful exhaust gases into nontoxic substances. It is also used in electronics, dentistry, medicine, hydrogen purification and jewelry. Ore deposits are rare; the most extensive lie in South Africa, Montana, Ontario and Russia. Recycling, mostly of scrapped catalytic converters, is also a major source.

Small wild cat of Central Asian mountains, also called the manul. Pallas's cat (*Otocolobus manul*) has long, dense, light gray fur and low-set rounded ears. Its head-and-body length is 46–65 cm (18–26 in), with a bushy tail of 21–31 cm (8.3–12.2 in). It inhabits rocky montane grasslands and shrublands from the Caucasus and Iran to Mongolia and Tibet, where it shelters in rock crevices and burrows and preys mainly on lagomorphs and rodents. Peter Simon Pallas first described it in 1776 near [[Lake Baikal]]. Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List since 2020, it is threatened locally by poaching and habitat fragmentation.

Interdisciplinary medical approach to relieving and preventing suffering in people with serious, complex and often terminal illnesses. The term comes from Latin *palliare*, to cloak. Palliative care aims to optimize quality of life and reduce suffering, and it can be given alongside curative treatment. Since the 2000s the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) has advocated applying its principles early in any chronic, ultimately fatal illness, rather than only at the end of life. Care is ideally delivered by teams that may include physicians, nurses, therapists, psychologists, social workers, chaplains and dietitians, in hospitals, outpatient clinics or at home. Historically focused on incurable [[Cancer|cancer]], it is now also applied to severe [[Heart failure|heart failure]], [[Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease|chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]] and [[Multiple sclerosis|multiple sclerosis]]. An estimated 40 million people a year need palliative care, about 78% of them in low- and middle-income countries, but only 14% of that population can receive it.

Ancient oasis city in central Syria and a caravan center on the [[Silk Road]]. Archaeological finds date to the Neolithic period, and documents first mention the city in the early 2nd millennium BC. Its merchants, the Palmyrenes, grew wealthy from trade caravans and founded colonies across the [[Roman Empire]]; their wealth paid for the Great Colonnade, the Temple of Bel and distinctive tower tombs. Palmyra became a subject of Rome in the 1st century AD. It reached its height in the 260s under King Odaenathus, who defeated the Sasanian emperor Shapur I. His widow [[Zenobia]] rebelled against Rome and established the Palmyrene Empire. In 273 the Roman emperor Aurelian leveled the city, which [[Diocletian]] later restored at a reduced size. In 2015 the [[Islamic State]] captured Palmyra and destroyed large parts of the ancient city; the Syrian Army recaptured it on 2 March 2017.

Canadian-American actress, model and media personality. She became known as a *Playboy* model, appearing as the magazine's February 1990 Playmate of the Month, and gained international fame as C.J. Parker on the drama series *Baywatch* (1992–1997). A 1995 sex tape, made from stolen home videos, led to a legal fight. Her later roles include Vallery Irons in *V.I.P.* (1998–2002) and the film *Scary Movie 3* (2003). In 2022 she made her Broadway debut as Roxie Hart in *Chicago*. She has supported [[Animal rights|animal rights]], particularly through People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), and endorses plant-based cooking.

Fertile low grasslands of southern South America, in [[Argentina]], Uruguay and southern Brazil. The name comes from Quechua *pampa*, meaning plain. The Argentine provinces of Buenos Aires, La Pampa, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and Córdoba lie within the region, which is interrupted only by low hills such as the Ventana and Tandil hills. The climate is temperate, with 600 to 1,200 mm (23.6 to 47.2 in) of precipitation spread fairly evenly through the year, which makes the soils suited to [[Agriculture|agriculture]]. Humans have changed the ecoregion, especially since [[Cattle|cattle]], pigs and above all sheep were released onto the plains. Summer days generally reach 28 to 33 °C (82 to 91 °F), while frost is frequent and snow is rare. The highest point, Cerro Tres Picos, reaches 1,239 m (4,065 ft).

United States airline (1927–1991). Pan American World Airways, founded in 1927, was the largest international air carrier for much of the 20th century and the first airline to fly worldwide. It introduced the first American jetliner, the [[Boeing 707]], in 1958, and later flew the [[Boeing 747]]. Its primary hub was the Worldport at [[John F. Kennedy International Airport]] in New York City. In 1970 it flew 11 million passengers to 86 countries. Pan Am faced rising competition after U.S. airline deregulation in 1978, failed restructuring attempts in the 1980s, and bankruptcy in 1991. It ceased operations on December 4, 1991.

Terrorist bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland. On 21 December 1988 a bomb destroyed the [[Boeing 747]] operating the flight from Frankfurt to Detroit via London and New York City, killing 243 passengers, 16 crew members and 11 residents of Lockerbie, 270 people in all. In 2001 Abdelbaset al-Megrahi, a Libyan, was found guilty of 270 counts of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. He was released on compassionate grounds in 2009 and died in 2012. In 2003 Libyan leader [[Muammar Gaddafi]] paid more than US$2 billion in compensation to victims' families, although he maintained that he never personally ordered the attack.

Network of roads about 30,000 km (19,000 mi) long across the Americas. It runs from Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, to Ushuaia, Argentina, and connects 14 countries, including [[Canada]], [[Mexico]], [[Panama]] and [[Colombia]]. The highway is interrupted by the Darién Gap, a roadless rainforest 106 km (66 mi) wide between Panama and Colombia, so North and South America are not linked by road. Construction proceeded in stages, beginning with a highway from Laredo, Texas, to [[Mexico City]], followed by the Inter-American Highway to Panama City. Panama, Colombia and environmentalists oppose building a road through the gap.

Spanish-language dark fantasy film directed by [[Guillermo del Toro]] and released in 2006. Its original title is *El laberinto del fauno*. Set in [[Francoist Spain]] in 1944, the film follows Ofelia, whose stepfather, Captain Vidal, hunts Maquis guerrillas, as she is drawn into a mythical world centered on an abandoned labyrinth and a faun. It is a co-production of Spain and Mexico. It premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May 2006, received a 22-minute standing ovation, and grossed $83 million worldwide. It won three [[Academy Awards]] and three BAFTA Awards.

Country at the southern end of Central America, on a narrow isthmus between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Its capital and largest city is [[Panama City]], whose metropolitan area holds nearly half of the country's more than 4 million people. Spanish colonists arrived in the 16th century. Panama broke away from Spain in 1821, joined [[Gran Colombia]], and seceded from Colombia in 1903 with United States backing, which allowed the construction of the [[Panama Canal]]. Canal tolls remain a significant part of the economy, alongside commerce, banking and tourism. Panama ranked 57th on the Human Development Index in 2019. Jungles cover about 40 percent of its land area and shelter many plants and animals found nowhere else on Earth. Panama is a founding member of the [[United Nations]].

Artificial waterway 82 km (51 mi) long across the Isthmus of Panama, linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Locks lift ships to Gatun Lake, an artificial freshwater lake 26 m (85 ft) above sea level created by damming the Chagres River, and lower them on the far side. The original locks allow passage of Panamax ships. A third, wider set of locks was built between September 2007 and May 2016, and the expanded canal began commercial operation on 26 June 2016, accommodating larger Neopanamax ships. The canal avoids the long, hazardous route around South America via the [[Drake Passage]]. French work began in 1881 but stopped in 1889. The United States took over in 1904 and opened the canal on 15 August 1914, and Panama took full control in 1999. A single ship passage uses an average of 200,000,000 liters of fresh water, so droughts threaten the canal.

Capital and largest city of Panama, at the Pacific entrance to the [[Panama Canal]]. Founded on 15 August 1519 by Spanish conquistador Pedro Arias Dávila, it was a launching point for the conquest of the [[Inca Empire]] and a transit point for gold and silver shipped to Spain across the isthmus. In 1671 the privateer Henry Morgan sacked and burned the original city. Its ruins, known as Panamá Viejo, are a [[World Heritage Site]]. The city was reestablished in 1673 about 8 km (5 miles) away, on the peninsula where the Casco Viejo historic quarter now stands. Panama City is the political and administrative center of the country and a hub for banking and commerce. Its metropolitan area has over 2,100,000 people.

Japanese multinational electronics manufacturer, headquartered in Kadoma, Osaka. Kōnosuke Matsushita founded the company in 1918 as Matsushita Electric Housewares Manufacturing Works. Its early products included radios, electric irons and bicycle lamps, sold under the National brand. The Panasonic brand was first adopted in 1955 for export markets. In the late 20th century the company overtook [[Philips]] to become the world's largest manufacturer of consumer electronics. It changed its name to Panasonic Corporation in 2008 and became Panasonic Holdings Corporation in 2022, when it reorganized as a holding company. Its products include rechargeable batteries, automotive and avionic systems, and home construction.

Family of twin-engine, variable-sweep-wing multirole combat aircraft. Developed by Panavia Aircraft GmbH, a consortium of British Aerospace, MBB of West Germany and Aeritalia of Italy. It first flew on 14 August 1974 and entered service in 1979–1980. Its main variants are the IDS (interdictor/strike) fighter-bomber, the ECR electronic combat and reconnaissance aircraft, and the ADV air defense interceptor. The Tornado served in the [[Gulf War]] of 1991 and in the [[Bosnian War]], [[Kosovo War]] and [[Iraq War]]. It is the only non-American-developed aircraft approved to carry United States nuclear weapons under [[NATO]]'s Nuclear Planning Group. A total of 990 aircraft were built.

Ancient Indian collection of interrelated animal fables in Sanskrit verse and prose, arranged within a frame story. The title means *Five Treatises*. The author is unknown: some recensions name Vishnu Sharma and others Vasubhaga, both possibly fictitious. Scholars consider it a Hindu text based on older oral traditions. It is among the most frequently translated literary works from India, with about 200 versions in more than 50 languages. The earliest known non-Indian translation, into Middle Persian, was made by Burzoe around 550 CE. An Arabic version, *Kalīlah wa Dimnah*, followed in 750 CE. Most European versions derive from a 12th-century Hebrew version by Rabbi Joel. Versions are also found in [[Indonesia]], [[Laos]] and [[Thailand]].

Mexican revolutionary, guerrilla leader and politician. Born José Doroteo Arango Arámbula, Villa was a key figure in the [[Mexican Revolution]], commanding the Division of the North in northern Mexico. A supporter of land reform, he was provisional governor of Chihuahua from 1913 to 1914. After breaking with Venustiano Carranza and allying with [[Emiliano Zapata]], he was defeated in 1915 by the Constitutionalist general Álvaro Obregón. In March 1916 he raided Columbus, New Mexico, prompting a U.S. expedition into Mexico that failed to capture him. In 1920 he negotiated an amnesty and a landed estate on condition that he retire from politics. He was assassinated in 1923. Mexicans often regard him as a hero who stood up to the United States, while some American media describe him as a villain. In 1976 his remains were reburied in the Monument to the Revolution in [[Mexico City]].

Organ of the digestive and endocrine systems of vertebrates, lying behind the stomach. Most of the pancreas is exocrine. It secretes pancreatic juice into the duodenum, where bicarbonate neutralizes stomach acid and digestive enzymes break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats. About 1 percent is endocrine, and its cells secrete the hormones [[Insulin|insulin]], glucagon, somatostatin and pancreatic polypeptide, which mainly regulate blood sugar. The human pancreas is about 12–15 cm (4.7–5.9 in) long and is divided into head, neck, body and tail. Inflammation of the pancreas, pancreatitis, is commonly caused by chronic alcohol use or gallstones. Because of its role in blood sugar regulation, the pancreas is central to [[Diabetes|diabetes]]. Its role in insulin production was identified in 1921.

Cancer arising in the pancreas, most often an adenocarcinoma of the ductal cells. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, which begins in the ducts that carry digestive enzymes, accounts for about 90% of cases. Neuroendocrine tumors, which arise from hormone-producing cells, make up 1–2%. Risk factors include [[Tobacco smoking|tobacco smoking]], obesity, diabetes and inherited genes. Surgery is the only treatment that can cure adenocarcinoma, and [[Palliative care|palliative care]] is recommended early even for patients receiving curative treatment. Nine percent of patients survive five years after diagnosis globally, and 14% in the United States. The disease caused 508,532 deaths worldwide in 2021.

Genus of palm-like, dioecious monocot trees and shrubs, with about 578 accepted species. Native to the Old World tropics and subtropics, they are called pandan, screw palm or screw pine, though they are not closely related to palms. Most have stout trunks supported by thick stilt roots, and crowns of strap-shaped leaves that may be spiny, from 30 cm (12 in) to 2 m (6.5 ft) long. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. The fruit is a cluster of drupes 10–20 cm (4–8 in) across that resembles a pineapple and turns from green to bright orange or red as it ripens. The oldest credible fossil, *Pandanus estellae*, is a silicified fruit from Queensland, Australia, dating to the Oligocene epoch around 32–28 million years ago. Species diversity is highest in [[Madagascar]] and [[Malaysia]].

Epidemic of an infectious disease that spreads across a large region, often worldwide. A pandemic involves a sudden increase in cases and affects a substantial portion of the human population. Widespread endemic diseases with stable case numbers, such as seasonal influenza, are generally excluded. The word comes from Greek *pan*, meaning all, and *demos*, meaning people. The [[Black Death]], caused by plague, killed up to half of Europe's population in the 14th century. The 1918 H1N1 influenza pandemic, known as the Spanish flu, is the deadliest in history. More recent pandemics include HIV/AIDS, the 2009 swine flu pandemic and the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. In May 2025 the [[World Health Organization]] adopted a pandemic agreement, approved with 120 votes in favor and 70 abstentions, without the United States, which had withdrawn from the organization.

Quaking aspen clone in [[Utah]], the world's largest tree by weight and landmass. Pando is a male clone of *Populus tremuloides* in Sevier County, within Fishlake National Forest. Its estimated 47,000 stems are genetically identical parts of one root system spanning 42.8 ha (106 acres). The name is Latin for *I spread*. Pando was identified in 1976 by Jerry Kemperman and Burton V. Barnes, and in 1992 researchers from the University of Colorado described it as a single male clone. By single-stem volume, the General Sherman Tree is the largest.
